INTRO01: P-101A identifies the physical pump that leaked in the north pump room.
Past work against P-101A helps the supervisor count leaks on this particular unit.
The repair order connects the reported leak to what the technician did and how many hours it took.
The issue records the seal taken from stores for this repair. The technician records whether it was installed.
INTRO02: The delivered pump will have its own installation and repair history.
Its serial number lets a technician recognize that same physical pump after a move.
The box contains interchangeable spares used to repair pumps.
Receiving adds seals to the balance. Issuing one for a repair subtracts one from that balance.
INTRO03: At the beginning of the example, P-101A occupies CW-DUTY in the north pump room.
Look up P-101A to see repairs carried out on the removed unit, including its earlier seal repair.
After the swap, the cooling-water system still needs the same duty position in the same room.
P-101B now occupies CW-DUTY. Its own asset record identifies work performed on the incoming pump.
INTRO04: A receipt links the delivered serial number to the purchase. The unit can still be awaiting installation.
Record the duty position, acceptance check and date the standby pump enters service.
Each inspection or repair adds evidence of condition, downtime and cost during the service period.
Record when and why the pump left service. Its earlier work remains available for replacement decisions.
INTRO05: The operator identifies the leak, its time, the duty position and the pump installed there.
A planner reviews the request, defines the repair activity and sets a seal aside if needed.
Stores records the seal taken for that order. A prior reservation only set it aside.
The technician enters hours, the work performed and the result so the completed repair can be traced.
INTRO06: The reason for starting the work determines which record and evidence to look for.
The leaking seal is an observed fault. Raise corrective work and retain the reported symptom.
In the example, a 30-day schedule sets up recurring inspections. Each generated order covers one occurrence.
A rising vibration reading prompts a review against the plant’s approved limit and follow-up rules.
INTRO07: WO-214 closed on 5 May. Use its completion date to locate the finished repair.
In this example, two hours at 40 plus one seal at 18 gives a recorded direct cost of 98.
The schedule lists an inspection for 2 June. Check its due date when looking ahead.
Keep the future inspection separate when totaling actual costs from completed work and posted transactions.
L001: Find the installed EAM release before looking up the planner’s work-order action.
Open the documentation for that release so field names and prerequisites match the application.
Find the release-work-order topic and compare its steps with the controls on the planner’s screen.
L002: Search the part list first so the storekeeper can locate a part that already exists.
Use the part code and organization to distinguish similarly named records.
Read the selected record and its message bar before editing the part or using a toolbar action.
L003: Inspect the toolbar for the action the planner wants to perform on the current record.
Read the command’s tooltip and confirm its effect before using it repeatedly.
Look up the documented key combination for that same action in the installed release.
Try the combination on a training record and check whether the browser intercepts the keys.
L004: Open My Account to review settings available to this user.
Choose the working language, save it and check labels when the session reopens.
Apply a permitted display or accessibility preference and inspect the affected screen.
L005: Select the pump by its equipment identifier before opening its documents.
Open the linked manual and check the approved revision and equipment model.
Keep the dated inspection report accessible from the unit it describes so later reviewers can retrieve it.
L006: Attach the note to the specific inspection that was deferred.
The author tells a planner whom to ask about the deferral.
The entry date places the note in the sequence of work on the inspection.
State the observed reason for deferral so another technician can understand the next step.
L007: Identify the controlled record and the field or status change the auditor needs to trace.
For an action configured to require a signature, follow the signature prompt for that action.
Check the recorded signer, date and action against the change under review.
L008: Start from a work-order list containing known examples both inside and outside the desired view.
Copy the Dataspy and set its status and due-date criteria for the planner’s backlog.
Run the saved view and check whether a known overdue order appears and a known closed order is excluded.
L009: Describe the installation in terms of its place, its duty and the unit carrying out that duty.
The room tells a technician where to go, including after a replacement.
The position identifies the duty successive pumps perform at the same installation.
The serialized pump carries its own service history when it moves to another duty.
L010: Identify the plant that owns the new equipment and check the user can access it.
Check that the intended department, class and other lookup values exist in that organization.
Create one representative unit and inspect its ownership and classification before entering the rest.
L011: Assign a class to group equipment with similar characteristics, such as pumps.
The class helps select attributes and relevant codes for this equipment family.
Select an approved closing code when recording the outcome of the repair.
The closing code lets reviewers compare the recorded outcomes of similar pump jobs.
L012: Open the asset for the particular serialized pump at PLANT01.
The asset identifier is the code used to find that unit in EAM, such as PUMP-001.
Compare the serial number with the delivered unit to distinguish two pumps of the same model.
Record where the pump is installed so a technician can connect the asset with its current duty.
L013: Create a position for a service that must continue when a unit is replaced.
CW-DUTY is an example position code that can be used to trace successive installations.
The installation link identifies which physical asset currently fills the duty.
In the diagram P-101B is the replacement unit. Its own asset history follows it after a later move.
L014: Use a system record to group equipment that delivers the cooling-water service.
Link the pump that moves the cooling water so its role is visible in the system hierarchy.
Include the drive motor when it is tracked as a component of the cooling system.
The pipework carries water through the system. Check its parent before using hierarchy totals.
L015: A location describes a physical place where assets can be found.
The building record supplies the broader site context when rooms have similar names.
Choose the actual pump room so a technician can find the installation.
L016: Choose the pipeline and an agreed measurement origin and direction before marking the work segment.
In the diagram, kilometre 12 identifies the beginning of the affected section.
The end reference identifies how far along the same linear asset the job extends.
With the same origin and direction, kilometres 12 to 14 describe a two-kilometre section.
L017: Associate the supplier agreement with the equipment to which it actually applies.
Check whether the failed component is listed or included under the agreement.
Compare the failure date and any usage limits with the recorded coverage window.
Review exclusions, supporting evidence and supplier requirements before preparing a claim.
L018: Capture the bearing failure and identify the equipment and supporting work order.
Match the failed item, date and operating conditions to the supplier’s warranty terms.
Associate the repair evidence with the claim and follow its status through the supplier review.
L019: The system groups the equipment delivering cooling water and gives the hierarchy a service context.
Check which components belong under the pump assembly before rolling up its work or costs.
Look up the control panel’s actual parent so it appears under the correct installation.
L020: Start from the system whose equipment structure the planner wants to check.
Expand the immediate children and look for the expected assemblies and their components.
Read the motor’s identifier and parent record before deciding whether its hierarchy link needs correction.
L021: Identify the installed measuring device and its unit before interpreting a change in reading.
A replacement device can start from a different reading. Keep its identity and changeover evidence.
The logical meter represents the equipment usage being tracked across readings.
Review cumulative equipment hours and the device change together before calculating the next service.
L022: The example starts at 910 hours on Monday. Use this as the first dated reading.
Wednesday’s 932 hours add 22 hours since Monday, using the same meter and unit.
Friday’s 951 hours add another 19. A later drop would warrant a check for a reset or entry error.
L023: Check ownership, open work and transfer restrictions while the asset is still at its original plant.
Record the unit’s code and serial number at the sending site so it can be identified at receipt.
Review the target organization and the resulting ownership after the authorized transfer.
Confirm that the receiving site can find the same unit and trace its earlier history.
L024: Review the approved pump-package configuration and the children it is intended to create.
Generate a sample package using the planned organization and identifier settings.
Inspect the new unit and its child links for omissions or duplicate identifiers before repeating the process.
L025: Record the operational and safety consequences for each pump using the agreed questions.
Apply the approved scoring weights to the recorded answers.
Compare the resulting priorities with engineering judgment and investigate unexpected rankings.
L026: USD identifies the currency used on a dollar-denominated quote.
An example amount of 100 USD retains its currency when the quote is compared with others.
EUR identifies a separate currency that can appear on a supplier’s offer.
To compare 100 EUR with a dollar quote, use the organization’s approved conversion rate and date.
L027: Use the supplier’s batch reference to distinguish one group of seals from another.
Capture the lot on receipt so a recalled batch can be traced to its entry into stock.
Review stock by part, store and lot to locate the remaining affected seals.
Retain the lot on an applicable issue so reviewers can trace where that batch was used.
L028: Two boxes arrive in the diagram. Confirm the purchase unit on the receipt.
The example conversion is ten individual seals in each box. Check the direction of the factor.
Two boxes times ten gives 20 seals in the stock unit. Compare the resulting unit cost as well.
L029: The store identifies who controls this stock and where replenishment is managed.
Bins divide the store into individual holding places used during picking and receipts.
Read the balance for the intended part and store when deciding whether to place an order.

Use the approved part code, such as SEAL-25, on the store association and transactions.
Describe the size or model clearly enough for a buyer to distinguish similar seals.
Set the unit used to count this part so receipts, issues and balances reconcile.

Record the area-clear observation as required by the approved checklist.
